title: sanstun brings a parallel-friendly sans-IO WireGuard to Rust
excerpt: sanstun is a Rust WireGuard state machine that separates I/O from core logic for easier testing and better performance.
body:
A few months into Firezone’s development the team hit a wall with boringtun. The fork kept growing: more than 70 pull requests landed just to stay compatible while the product needed new behaviours. One early change was to make time handling fully sans-IO, adding `_at`-suffixed APIs that accept an `Instant`. That patch alone showed how tightly the original library was tied to its own side-effects. As requirements kept shifting, keeping 100 % API compatibility with upstream became a maintenance nightmare.

The team decided to stop patching and start fresh. The result is sanstun, a WireGuard state machine written in Rust that follows the sans-IO philosophy from the ground up. By separating all I/O, randomness and timing from the core logic, the library composes cleanly, is easy to test, and works nicely with Rust’s ownership model. The post walks through why the move happened, the core API pieces, and what it means to drop internal buffering.

## Why the team moved away from boringtun

Boringtun did the job at first, but the Firezone team kept adding patches for bug fixes and new features. Each patch introduced a new API or changed an existing one, and the team tried to keep the original API stable so upstream could still accept their changes. Over two years this approach proved unsustainable.  

The first major friction point was time handling. Boringtun originally used its own clock, which made deterministic testing hard. The team introduced a fully sans-IO time layer by adding `_at` variants that accept an explicit `Instant`. While that solved the testing issue, it also illustrated how tightly the library’s internals were coupled to side-effects.  

A second pain spot was internal buffering. Boringtun would automatically create a session when a packet arrived without an existing one, storing the packet until the handshake completed. Draining that buffer required calling `decapsulate` with a zero-length datagram, a pattern that feels unintuitive, forces extra allocations, and hides the buffer size from the caller.

The Firezone team flagged this behaviour and eventually decided that the library should not buffer at all. Removing the buffer simplified the contract: the caller now decides when and how to store packets that cannot be sent immediately.

These two issues, tight coupling to time and hidden buffering, made the library hard to evolve. By starting over with sanstun, the team could design an API that matches the real needs of a userspace WireGuard implementation without legacy baggage.

## Key sans-IO API building blocks

Sanstun’s public surface mirrors the four WireGuard message types: handshake initiation, handshake response, cookie reply, and encrypted data. Each type has a dedicated entry point, keeping the flow explicit.

* Inbound handling, `Tunnel::handle_handshake_initiation` processes a received handshake initiation. After parsing, the library returns a state that the caller can feed into `Tunnel::begin_decapsulate` and later `Tunnel::commit_decapsulate` to produce the decrypted payload.  
* Outbound handling, `Tunnel::begin_encapsulate` prepares an encrypted packet for sending. The caller receives the ciphertext and is responsible for transmitting it over the network.  
* Timer updates, `Tunnel::handle_timeout` lets the caller inform the tunnel that a deadline has passed, while `Tunnel::poll_timeout` asks the tunnel when the next timeout should occur. Both use explicit `Instant` values, keeping time completely under the caller’s control.  

Because the API never hides side-effects, testing becomes straightforward: a test can feed a deterministic sequence of timestamps and packets and verify the exact output without any hidden network or clock calls.

## Eliminating internal buffering for a cleaner contract

The most visible change from boringtun to sanstun is the removal of automatic buffering. In the old library, sending a packet when no session existed would silently queue the packet until the handshake finished. The queue drained only when the caller invoked `decapsulate` with an empty datagram, a step that many developers missed, leading to stuck packets and unexpected memory use.

Sanstun forces the caller to handle that case explicitly. To send a packet, the code calls `Tunnel::begin_encapsulate`. If there is no active session, the call returns an error indicating that a handshake is required. The caller must then either buffer the packet itself or start a handshake with `Tunnel::initiate_handshake`. This design makes the contract obvious: the library never assumes it can store data for you.

A concrete example illustrates the flow:

```rust
let result = tunnel.begin_encapsulate(&packet);
match result {
    Ok(ciphertext) => send_over_udp(ciphertext),
    Err(NoSession) => {
        // Caller buffers the packet until a session is ready
        pending_packets.push(packet);
        // Start a handshake so the session can be established
        tunnel.initiate_handshake(peer_public_key);
    }
}
```

The caller decides how large the `pending_packets` buffer should be, when to drop old entries, and how to prioritize retransmissions. This approach eliminates the hidden allocation that boringtun performed and aligns with the sans-IO principle that all side-effects live outside the core logic.

## The takeaway

Sanstun replaces a heavily patched boringtun fork with a clean, sans-IO WireGuard state machine. By moving time handling and randomness out of the library and by removing internal buffering, the API becomes explicit, testable, and easier to evolve.

When sending data, the caller now buffers packets themselves if no session exists, using `Tunnel::begin_encapsulate` as the single entry point for outbound traffic. This contract gives developers full control over memory, timing, and error handling, which is the core advantage of the new design.
